sentences: A woman holds a small child firmly on her lap and washes the child's foot in the basin below.
The American painter Mary Cassatt made this picture in 1893, and it belongs to the Art Institute of Chicago.
Cassatt worked in Paris and was the only American artist to exhibit with the French Impressionists.
Moments of physical closeness between a woman and a child, full of intimacy, were her signature subject.
Pattern fills the picture, from wallpaper and painted furniture to clothing and floor.
It reflects her intense engagement with Japanese art after she saw Japanese woodblock prints in Paris in 1890.
She especially admired a bathing scene by Utamaro.
Look at the two heads, one with dark hair pinned up and one with a short fringe.
Woman and child bow together, gazing down at the same spot.
Their faces are half hidden, so we quietly watch how absorbed they are.
One of the woman's hands wraps around the child's belly, holding the child steady.
A white cloth circles the child's middle, and a bent arm helps keep the balance.
The two bodies press together as a single form.
Her dress has bold vertical stripes of green, pink and white that run all the way down to the floor.
The steep viewpoint from above makes the space shallow, so the carpeted floor seems to stand upright on the surface of the canvas.
Cassatt took this sharp angle and the bathing subject from her friend Degas.
Now look lower.
The woman's hand holds the child's foot and washes it in the water, and this point where hand meets foot is the heart of the painting.
Look at the floor in the lower left, below the woman's arm.
There, in blue paint, she signed her name, Mary Cassatt.
It blends quietly into the carpet pattern, so it is fun to search for.
Notice the round basin and the reflections on the water.
Its oval echoes the rounded heads of the two figures, and the flowered water jug at the right makes a pair with it.
Both of their gazes fall right here, onto the water.
The painting was first shown at her exhibition at the Galeries Durand-Ruel in Paris in 1893.
It was widely exhibited after that, and the Art Institute of Chicago bought it in 1910.
After Cassatt died in 1926, the museum hung it again that December in a memorial exhibition.
Now step back and look with them at the water below.
Before this quiet, ordinary moment, what is the first thing you feel?
